title: Middleware Patterns
description: Understand the chain of responsibility pattern in web servers, how Express and FastAPI middleware pipelines work, cross-cutting concerns, and middleware ordering bugs that cause production incidents.

segments.text: Every production web server runs a pipeline of middleware: authentication, logging, rate limiting, compression, CORS. These are cross-cutting concerns that apply to most requests. Getting the middleware pipeline right is straightforward. Getting it wrong causes subtle bugs that are incredibly hard to diagnose.

Middleware implements the chain of responsibility pattern. Each middleware receives the request, does its work, and either passes to the next handler or short-circuits the chain. Authentication middleware checks the token — valid, pass it along; invalid, return 401 immediately. The request flows through a pipeline of these handlers.

In Express.js, middleware is a function taking request, response, and next. Calling next passes to the next middleware. Not calling next stops the chain. The order you register middleware with app.use determines execution order. This seems simple, but the implicit ordering creates a class of bugs I see in every Node.js codebase.

Classic ordering bug: a team added rate limiting middleware after the authentication middleware. Unauthenticated requests hit the rate limiter, but attackers could brute-force the login endpoint without being rate-limited because auth failure responses short-circuited before reaching the rate limiter's response tracking.
Consider this middleware stack: body parser, CORS, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, logging, compression, your route handler. Is this order correct? What would you change?
segments.thought_prompt: What's the ideal ordering for these middleware? Think about what needs to run before what.

segments.text: The correct order: rate limiting first to protect all endpoints, then CORS for browser preflight handling, logging to capture all requests including rejected ones, body parser to deserialize payloads, authentication, authorization, compression on the response, then your handler. Rate limiting must be outermost to prevent abuse.

FastAPI takes a different approach with dependency injection. Instead of a linear chain, dependencies are declared per route. An auth dependency runs only on routes that need it. This eliminates ordering bugs but requires discipline: forgetting to add the auth dependency to a new endpoint is an open security hole.

Error handling middleware must be the outermost wrapper. In Express, an error-handling middleware has four parameters: error, request, response, next. If any middleware throws and nobody catches it, the server returns a 500 with potentially sensitive stack traces. In production, this has leaked database credentials in error messages.

Each middleware adds latency. On a typical Express stack with ten middleware layers, you're adding one to three milliseconds of overhead per request. That sounds small, but at 10,000 requests per second, it's significant. Profile your middleware: I've seen logging middleware using synchronous JSON serialization that added 5 milliseconds per request.

Common cross-cutting middleware patterns: request ID injection for distributed tracing, where each request gets a unique ID propagated through headers. Tenant context extraction for multi-tenant apps. Request timeout enforcement to prevent hanging connections. Circuit breaker middleware that short-circuits when downstream services are unhealthy.

A team deployed middleware that validated JWT tokens by calling an external auth service. Under load, the auth service became slow. Every incoming request blocked waiting for JWT validation. The entire server ground to a halt because middleware was synchronously blocking the event loop with an HTTP call to a degraded service.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you design auth middleware that doesn't create a hard dependency on an external service?

segments.text: Middleware order matters more than most teams realize. Put security-critical middleware outermost. Error handling wraps everything. Profile each layer's latency contribution. And never make synchronous calls to external services in the middleware pipeline — cache tokens locally and validate signatures offline.
